node.label: C. A. Bayly
node.date_label: Rulers, Townsmen and Bazaars (1983) · Empire and Information (1996) · The Birth of the Modern World (2004)
node.description: Historian of South Asia and empire whose global comparisons retained local and regional foundations. In Binu M. John’s interview Bayly explains modernity as interacting changes across several societies rather than a single Western essence. He also challenges accounts of an all-powerful colonial state by emphasizing Indian intermediaries and the uneven development of British rule. These positions coexist with his explicit refusal to identify only as a global historian.

named_group_routes.relationship: Subaltern Studies essays treat peasant, tribal and worker action under colonial rule as politics with its own forms, and are criticised for overstating its autonomy (1982–88)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997, pp. 86–87, read against the page images) lists early work that explored 'popular or subaltern autonomy in action, consciousness and culture': Hardiman on the peasant nationalists of Gujarat, Pandey on Congress organization and peasant militancy, Amin on rumours of Gandhi, studies of 'tribal movements and cults' and of Bengal labour. Bayly (1988; Verso reprint pp. 116–126, read) finds the essays' empirical work strong but holds that 'their concern to emphasize peasant autonomy seems to have deflected them from moving towards a “total history”' (p. 121) and that 'Simply to stress that autonomy ... is not very helpful in any attempt to specify the nature of historical change' (p. 126). O'Hanlon (1988; reprint pp. 85–86) criticises the 'literal interpretation of subaltern autonomy' in several contributions (Henningham, Ramachandra Guha, Dasgupta) while setting Ranajit Guha's book apart (p. 85). Ranajit Guha's own argument is the separate edge from his person entry.

named_group_routes.relationship: The programme statement of Subaltern Studies: a critique of colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism, an autonomous but overlapping domain of 'the politics of the people', and a method of reading rebel consciousness through counter-insurgency records (1982–83)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Preface to Subaltern Studies I (dated Canberra, August 1981), read in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (Oxford, 1988), p. 35: the series is to 'rectify the elitist bias characteristic of much research and academic work' in South Asian studies; 'subaltern' is taken in the Concise Oxford sense, 'of inferior rank', as 'a name for the general attribute of subordination in South Asian society whether this is expressed in terms of class, caste, age, gender and office or in any other way'. 'On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India' (same reprint, pp. 37–44; Subaltern Studies I pagination is pp. 1–8): elitist historiography 'is of course not without its uses' (p. 38) but 'fails to acknowledge, far less interpret, the contribution made by the people on their own, that is, independently of the elite' (p. 39); 'What clearly is left out of this un-historical historiography is the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain, for it neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', 'As modern as indigenous elite politics' (p. 40); the two domains were not 'hermetically sealed off'; 'there was a great deal of overlap' (p. 42); the same class 'dominant in one area ... could be among the dominated in another' (p. 44). He claims a direction, not a doctrine: 'Let a hundred flowers blossom and we don't mind even the weeds' (p. 43); 'We claim no more than to try and indicate an orientation' (p. 43). Method, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983), introduction read (Duke 1999 printing, which keeps the 1983 Oxford pagination): 'To acknowledge the peasant as the maker of his own rebellion is to attribute ... a consciousness to him' (p. 4); 'How then are we to get in touch with the consciousness of insurgency when our access to it is barred thus by the discourse of counter-insurgency?'; 'It should be possible therefore to read the presence of a rebel consciousness as a necessary and pervasive element within that body of evidence' (p. 15). 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency', Subaltern Studies II (Delhi, 1983), pp. 1–42, read in full: historiography takes the peasant rebel 'merely as an empirical person or member of a class, but not as an entity whose will and reason constituted the praxis called rebellion' (p. 2); 'Cause is made to stand in as a phantom surrogate for Reason' (p. 3); the historian should 'stop pretending that it can fully grasp a past consciousness and reconstitute it' (p. 33). In-period reception, a member's reading first: Spivak, 'Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography', Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363 (read): the group 'offers a theory of change' (p. 330); its practice is 'closer to deconstruction' (p. 332) and its presuppositions are 'not, strictly speaking, consonant with a desire to find a consciousness (here of the subaltern) in a positive and pure state' (p. 333); quoting Elementary Aspects p. 15, she reads 'the project to retrieve the subaltern consciousness' 'as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest' (pp. 341–342), which 'would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness' (p. 356); 'The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women' but overlooks 'how important the concept-metaphor woman is' (p. 356). Rosalind O'Hanlon, 'Recovering the Subject' (Modern Asian Studies 22:1, 1988, pp. 189–224; read in the Verso reprint, 2000, pp. 72–115, whose pages are cited): 'the classic figure of Western humanism—the self-originating, self-determining individual ... is readmitted through the back door in the figure of the subaltern himself' (p. 74). C. A. Bayly, 'Rallying Around the Subaltern' (Journal of Peasant Studies 16:1, 1988, pp. 110–120; Verso reprint pp. 116–126): the Subalterns 'acted mainly as a catalyst' for an existing minority interest (p. 116); Guha's approach 'seems sometimes to postulate the existence of an unchanging peasantry and unified peasant consciousness defined by struggle with colonialism' (p. 121). Sumit Sarkar, 'The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies' (1997; pp. 82–87 and 90–94 read, pp. 84–87 against the page images): the early volumes were 'largely ignored in the West' while debated in 'Left-leaning intellectual circles in India' (p. 84); 'it was argued with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' that anti-colonial movements had been explained 'far too often' by economic pressures and mobilization from the top (p. 85); the claims of a new 'paradigm' 'were certainly over-flamboyant' (p. 86); the theoretical turn 'had its origins in Guha's attempt to use some of the language and methods of Lévi-Straussian structuralism' (p. 87). Founder language is attributed, not adopted: Chakrabarty (1997) calls him 'the founder of the group' (subaltern source); Scott's foreword to the 1999 Duke printing writes that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document of what is now known as the Subaltern Studies School', adding that 'The term school conveys far too much in the way of a rigid orthodoxy' (p. ix). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (Nepantla, 2000) treats 'the work of the historian Ranajit Guha in the period when he acted as the founding editor' as 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11). edge_115 (subaltern → post) and edge_159 (gramsci → subaltern) stay.

sources.title: Ranajit Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983; Duke edition 1999).
sources.citation: Ranajit Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983; Duke edition 1999).

verification.note: Duke description and contents checked for insurgent consciousness, dominance/subordination, deliberate peasant political action and the original 1983 versus 1999 edition. James C. Scott wrote the later foreword. No full primary book read; a search-result PDF proved to be Banerjee’s different 2020 book and was excluded. The intervention does not certify homogeneous peasant consciousness or a single path to nationalism. Addendum 2026-10-14: Primary text now read for the Guha person entry. Introduction pp. 1–17 OCR'd at 300 dpi from a scan of the Duke University Press 1999 printing (foreword by James C. Scott) hosted by Berhampore Girls' College; preface dated Canberra, January 1983; the text keeps the 1983 Oxford pagination, checked against the Digital Library of India scan of the Delhi 1983 edition (Internet Archive dli.bengal.10689.12632; imprint 'First published 1983, Second impression 1986'). Quoted: 'Insurgency was thus the necessary antithesis of colonialism' (p. 2); 'a discourse of power'; the peasant 'denied recognition as a subject of history' (p. 3); 'a consciousness'; spontaneity 'elitist as well as erroneous' (p. 4); Gramsci on spontaneity; Hobsbawm's 'pioneering work' and 'pre-political' (p. 5); 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India'; 'nothing ... that was not political' (p. 6); 'a composite apparatus of dominance' (p. 8); 'negative and inversive procedure' (p. 9); limits that define 'the quality of that politics' (p. 10); 'inchoate and naive' (p. 11); Gramsci's 'pillars of politics' and 'elementary aspects' (p. 12); 'its sovereignty, its consistency and its logic' (p. 13); reading rebel consciousness in counter-insurgency records (pp. 14–15). Bibliography: Gramsci, Selections (1971); Hobsbawm, Primitive Rebels (Manchester, 1959); Hobsbawm and Rudé, Captain Swing (1969). Pp. 89–90 (Thompson on the Blacks; Hobsbawm's 'social banditry') read in the 1983 edition's text. Scott's foreword: Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document' of 'the Subaltern Studies School' (p. ix). The rest of the book is unread.

Note 1 thanks Gautam Bhadra, Dipesh Chakrabarty and Raghabendra Chattopadhyay. Reprint pages; Subaltern Studies I pagination (pp. 1–8) is cited by Sarkar and O'Hanlon.

sources.title: Sumit Sarkar, “The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies,” in Writing Social History (Oxford University Press, 1997).
sources.citation: Sumit Sarkar, “The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies,” in Writing Social History (Oxford University Press, 1997).

verification.note: Primary scan pp. 82–87 visually read; scan heading identifies Oxford 1997. Participant criticism identifies changing emphases and internal tensions, while crediting empirical achievements. P. 83 supplies named Thompson reception and footnoted borrowing claims; Guha’s cited passages and the rest of Sarkar’s essay remain unread. Sarkar’s diagnosis is not a neutral consensus. Addendum 2026-10-14: Scan OCR'd locally and pp. 84–85, 87 and 97 checked against the page images for the 1.132 person entry. Quoted: Chakrabarty's summary of a shift from 'to write “better” Marxist histories' to the problem of 'universalism/Eurocentrism' (pp. 84–85; Sarkar's n. 5 cites Chakrabarty's 'Marx after Marxism: Subaltern Histories and the Question of Difference', Polygraph 6/7, 1993, unread); 'the trajectory that has been outlined with considerable precision and frankness by Chakrabarty has been debilitating in both academic and political terms' (p. 85); 'Dipesh Chakrabarty’s stimulating, if controversial, essays on Bengal labour history' (p. 87; n. 10 names the Subaltern Studies II (1983) and III (1984) jute-worker essays); on kula and grihalaksmi, 'Beauty, pleasure, the good life ... for whom, it is surely legitimate to ask' (p. 97; n. 39 cites Chakrabarty's 'The Difference-Deferral of a Colonial Modernity: Public Debates on Domesticity in British Bengal', Subaltern Studies VIII, 1994, pp. 83–85, unread). Addendum 2026-10-14: Re-read for the Guha person entry: pp. 82–87 and 90–94 OCR'd, pp. 84–87 checked against the page images. Quoted: Guha's 1982 preface and essay 'full of references to “subaltern classes”, evocations of Gramsci' (p. 82); British Marxian social history 'probably the most significant' influence and Guha's 'subaltern' used 'somewhat in the way Thompson deployed the term “plebeian”' (p. 83; n. 3: Elementary Aspects 'frequently cited Thompson with approval', to Whigs and Hunters and Albion's Fatal Tree); the early volumes 'largely ignored in the West' (p. 84; n. 4 names O'Hanlon 1988 as Modern Asian Studies' first engagement); 'argued with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' (p. 85; n. 7: 'A more explicit critique of orthodox Marxist historiography was made by Guha' in 'The Prose of Counterinsurgency'); 'over-flamboyant' paradigm claims and the group's modification of 'the historiography of anticolonial nationalism' (p. 86); 'Guha's attempt to use some of the language and methods of Lévi-Straussian structuralism' (p. 87); Chatterjee's 'derivative discourses' (p. 91); 'an unnoticed drift implicit even in Guha's initial formulation' (p. 92); Guha's 'Chandra's Death' as a 'seldom-referred-to' alternative (pp. 93–94).

Primary AHA 1997 article consulted from opening through the discussion of disciplinary limits: Guha’s Santal example, Amin, and Telling the Truth About History. This is the 1997 web essay, not the 1998 journal version. Its claims about professional secular history remain Chakrabarty’s argument, not a consensus or a characterization of all Indigenous historical practice. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full for the 1.132 person entry in the Internet Archive capture of 16 July 2024 of the AHA page (byline Dipesh Chakrabarty; Publication Date November 1, 1997; Perspectives Section Viewpoints); the live page returned 403 to automated requests. Web text, no page numbers. Quoted: minority histories becoming 'additional instances of “good history”'; 'Let me call these histories subordinated or “subaltern” pasts'; 'pasts that resist historicization'; Guha as 'the founder of the group'; 'it is arguable that' Subaltern Studies differs from 'history from below' by 'the self-critical awareness of this problem'; the Santal statement 'has to be anthropologized'; 'the historian as historian, unlike the Santal, cannot invoke the supernatural in explaining/describing an event'.
